approved: Australian National Preventive Health Agency (Abolition) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would close the Australian National Preventive Health Agency.
Preventive health tasks shared between two federal bodies would be merged into the Department of Health to cut duplication and costs.
The bill would end the roles of the agency's chief executive, staff, advisory council and committees, and transfer leftover work to the Department of Health.
Repeals the Australian National Preventive Health Agency Act 2010.
Transfers the agency's functions to the Commonwealth Department of Health.
Terminates the positions of the chief executive, staff, advisory council and committees.
The Australian National Preventive Health Agency, its staff and advisory bodies, and the Commonwealth Department of Health.

Introduced the Australian National Preventive Health Agency (Abolition) Bill 2014, arguing ANPHA duplicated Department of Health functions and was funded solely by the Commonwealth, and that abolishing it would remove overlap and reintegrate its alcohol, tobacco and obesity work into the department without cutting funding commitments.

Detailed the case against abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, established in 2010 after task force consultations with almost 1,000 stakeholders, saying Labor invested nearly $1 billion in a national partnership agreement on prevention that the coalition has since cut by more than $360 million, and said downloads of the My QuitBuddy smoking-cessation app rose from 19,000 to 55,000 in a single month during the Summernats event that draws over 100,000 people.

Supported abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, criticising it for spending $463,000 on a fat tax study despite evidence from Denmark that such taxes fail, and for spending about $263,000 on a fake music festival Facebook campaign that received only 244 likes, roughly $1,000 per like of taxpayer money.

Opposed abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, citing data showing 672,000 hospital admissions in 2011-12 could have been avoided with better primary care, noting a smoking-cessation app saw downloads triple to 55,000 after an ANPHA-funded promotion at Summernats, and warned her Lalor electorate's Mercy Health service, built for 90,000 people, will soon serve 200,000.

Argued the Australian National Preventive Health Agency duplicates the work of the federal Department of Health and six state health departments, noting no state government had ever engaged the agency since the bill's announcement, calling it a waste of taxpayer money.

Reflected on health economics, noting Australia's $130 billion health system spends about 45 per cent of that on just two per cent of the population near the end of life, and argued the country's 35,000 general practitioners, trained for at least a decade, are the true front line for effective preventative health, not standalone agencies like ANPHA.

Opposed abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, cited a Lancet study showing one in three Australians, or 5.2 million people, are now obese, an 80 per cent rise in 33 years, and criticized the assistant health minister for scrapping a healthy-eating website built over two years on the advice of a staffer who was formerly an alcohol lobbyist.

Defended abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency as duplicative, since no state or territory government ever contributed funding to it, and credited existing Commonwealth efforts like the Measure Up campaign, running since 2006, for tobacco use falling by more than 40 per cent among both men and women over the past 33 years.

Supported abolishing the Australian National Preventive Health Agency, calling it a taxpayer-funded lobby group that both advocates for and receives government funding, citing an Institute of Public Affairs report finding a third of submissions to the original Preventative Health Taskforce came from bodies receiving large taxpayer funding.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, citing $360 million in cuts to preventive health national partnership funding, and warned the Good Start Program supporting Maori and Pasifika health in the electorate of Rankin, home to almost 14,000 New Zealand-born residents, would lose funding from 1 July.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, quoting the health minister's own second reading speech saying taxpayers should 'pick up the bill' for people who disregard health consequences, and highlighted men's health data showing men are four times more likely than women to die by suicide, an average of five a day.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, citing a study finding preventive programs on smoking, road safety and heart disease prevented about 400,000 premature deaths between 1975 and 1995, saving $8.4 billion, far more than the agency's own $6.4 million budget.

Opposed abolishing ANPHA, criticising the minister responsible for preventive health, Senator Fiona Nash, for removing the healthy food-rating website and employing a former fast-food industry lobbyist as chief of staff, and cited AMA figures that 90 per cent of Australians have tried alcohol and 83 per cent drank in the past 12 months.

Summed up the ANPHA abolition bill, saying the agency represented symbolism over substance, spending taxpayer money on things like sponsoring burnouts at Summernats, and that its preventive health functions would continue more efficiently within the Department of Health.
